fixes.explanation: That's the line, baker. Israel broke the yoke, tore off the chains and said, 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). A yoke is the heavy wooden bar that ties an ox to its work, so they were snapping loose from their load. That's a big announcement to make out loud.

Not quite, friend. Nobody in this verse asks for a new king. The words are 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). They weren't shopping for a replacement. They said they would not serve, and that's all the verse gives.

Price makes sense in a bakery, baker, but not here. The word is 'stain' (Jeremiah 2:22). The LORD says that even if they wash with lye and an abundance of soap, the stain of their guilt is still before Him. Soap is for stains, so the picture fits that word.

Yes, False. The LORD says, 'All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her' (Jeremiah 2:24). No long search needed. The picture is a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, sniffing the wind, and those who seek her will find her.

That's the word, baker. They say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth' (Jeremiah 2:27). That includes their kings, officials, priests and prophets (Jeremiah 2:26). They said it to wood and stone, and the LORD says they turned their backs to Him and not their faces.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, 'But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can' (Jeremiah 2:28). They'd made those gods themselves. So He challenges those gods to rise up and save Israel if they can.
That's it. 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). A bride doesn't forget her wedding sash, and yet they'd forgotten Him for that long. That's a long, long stretch.

Forty is a famous number in the Bible, but it's not this one. The LORD says, 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). Without number means no count is given at all. The verse leaves it at that.
Correct, baker. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Assyria let them down, and the same is said of Egypt. Same disappointment, new address.
I wish, friend, but no. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Just as. So Egypt is said to disappoint them the same way Assyria did.

That's a big plan, baker, but it isn't in the verse. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Egypt isn't said to defeat Assyria for them. The word is disappointed, the same as with Assyria.

That isn't what He says, baker. The LORD says, 'You will leave that place with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those you trust' (Jeremiah 2:37). He says they will not prosper by the help of those they trust. Hands on heads is how He says they leave.

That's the question, baker. The LORD says, 'you would return to Me?' (Jeremiah 3:1). He begins with a picture of a man who divorces his wife and she marries another, asking if he can ever return to her. Then He turns it on them, after saying they have played the harlot with many lovers. It's a heavy question, and it's the LORD asking it.

Yes, ashamed. The LORD says, 'you have the brazen look of a prostitute; you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). Earlier He said a thief is ashamed when he is caught (Jeremiah 2:26). He sets that beside Israel, who refuses to be ashamed.
Comforted sounds gentle, baker, but it's not the word. The LORD says, 'you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). The brazen look is the point. It's about shame, and the verse says they refused it.

Corrected is close in spirit, friend, but the verse says something else. The LORD says, 'you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). It's about shame, and the verse says they refused it. Back in Jeremiah 2:30, the trouble was that they accepted no discipline, so you can see how those fit together.
